derivations.claim: If the support columns indexed by $S(x)$ are dependent, choose a nonzero vector $d$ supported on $S(x)$ with $Ad=0$. Since each $x_j>0$ on this finite support, choose $\varepsilon>0$ smaller than $x_j/|d_j|$ for every nonzero $d_j$. Then $x+\varepsilon d$ and $x-\varepsilon d$ are distinct nonnegative solutions of $Az=b$, and their midpoint is $x$; hence $x$ is not extreme.

Suppose instead that the support columns are independent and $x=(u+v)/2$ for $u,v\in P(A,b)$. For $j\notin S(x)$, nonnegativity and $x_j=0$ force $u_j=v_j=0$. Thus $u-v$ is supported on $S(x)$ and $A(u-v)=0$; independence forces $u-v=0$, so $u=v=x$ and $x$ is extreme.

If the support columns of a feasible point are dependent, take $d$ as in step 1.1 and choose its sign so some $d_j<0$. With $t=\min_{d_j<0}x_j/(-d_j)>0$, the point $x+td$ remains feasible, remains nonnegative, and has strictly fewer positive coordinates. Repeating this support reduction at most $n$ times gives a feasible point whose support columns are independent.

Because $A$ has rank $m$, its columns span $\mathbb R^m$. Extend the independent support columns from step 2.1 to $m$ independent columns of $A$ by repeatedly taking the least-index column outside their current span; assigning zero to each added coordinate makes the reduced point the basic vector of that basis. It is therefore a basic feasible solution. When $m=0$, support reduction gives the zero vector and the empty list is the required basis.

A basic feasible solution has support contained in an independent basis, so its support columns are independent and step 1.2 makes it extreme. Conversely, an extreme feasible point has independent support by step 1.1 and extends to a basis by step 3.1. Thus the three stated conditions are equivalent, and step 3.1 proves existence whenever $P(A,b)$ is nonempty.

derivations.claim: Every pivot in [F3] uses a negative reduced cost and a nonnegative ratio, so [F2] makes the objective nonincreasing. If a basis repeats, the deterministic rule repeats the same future pivots and produces a cycle; the objective returns to its initial value, forcing every pivot decrease to be zero. Since each entering reduced cost is strictly negative, every pivot in the cycle has $\theta=0$, so the represented feasible vector stays fixed throughout the cycle.

Let $T$ be the indices that enter in this cycle and let $q=\max T$. Because the basis returns, $q$ also leaves. Choose a tableau $P$ where $q$ enters and a tableau $Q$ where $q$ leaves. At $P$, its reduced cost $r_q^P<0$ and $r_j^P\ge0$ for every $j<q$: a basic reduced cost is zero, and a lower-index eligible nonbasic variable would have been chosen instead. At $Q$, the entering variable $t$ is in $T$, is not the basic variable $q$, and therefore satisfies $t<q$.

At $Q$, put $d=A_{B_Q}^{-1}a_t$ and define the entering direction $z_t=1$, $z_{B_Q}=-d$, with other nonbasic coordinates zero. Then $Az=0$, $c^{\mathsf T}z=r_t^Q<0$, and $z_q<0$ because $q$ leaves through a row with positive pivot coefficient. If $r^P=c-A^{\mathsf T}y^P$ is the reduced-cost vector at $P$, then $r^P\cdot z=c^{\mathsf T}z<0$ since $Az=0$.

For every $j>q$, $r_j^Pz_j=0$: if $j$ is basic at $P$ then $r_j^P=0$, while if it is nonbasic at $P$, maximality of $q$ means it never enters during the cycle and it is nonbasic at $Q$, where $z_j=0$. Also $r_q^Pz_q>0$. Thus the negative sum $r^P\cdot z$ forces some $j<q$ with $r_j^Pz_j<0$; because $r_j^P\ge0$, this gives $r_j^P>0$ and $z_j<0$. Such a $j$ is nonbasic at $P$, basic at $Q$, and has $d_j>0$. Its value is zero at $P$ and stays zero during the degenerate cycle, so at $Q$ it ties with $q$ at ratio zero.
Since $j<q$ is an eligible leaving variable with the same minimum ratio as $q$, [F3] would choose $j$ to leave at $Q$, contradicting the choice of $q$. Therefore no basis repeats.

There are at most $\binom{n}{m}$ possible column bases, so the algorithm terminates after at most that many visited bases. At termination [F2] gives either an optimal basis or an unbounded ray. If the objective is bounded below, the ray branch is impossible. If the feasible set is nonempty, [F4] supplies a starting basis; hence a finite optimum is attained at an optimal basis found by the algorithm. The combinatorial bound does not imply polynomial-time complexity.

derivations.claim: Fix an eligible pivot $(i,j)$ and put $q=A_B^{-\mathsf T}e_i$. With $\alpha=\bar c_j/d_{ij}\le0$, the vector $y'=y+\alpha q$ satisfies $a_j^{\mathsf T}y'=c_j$, so the entering column has new reduced cost zero. The leaving basic column $a_{B_i}$ has $q^{\mathsf T}a_{B_i}=1$, hence its new reduced cost is $-\alpha\ge0$.

For any other nonbasic $k$, write $d_{ik}=q^{\mathsf T}a_k$. Its new reduced cost is $\bar c'_k=\bar c_k-\alpha d_{ik}$. If $d_{ik}\ge0$, this is nonnegative because $\alpha\le0$. If $d_{ik}<0$, the ratio rule gives $\bar c_j/(-d_{ij})\le\bar c_k/(-d_{ik})$, so $\bar c'_k=(-d_{ik})(\bar c_k/(-d_{ik})-\bar c_j/(-d_{ij}))\ge0$. Thus every new nonbasic reduced cost is nonnegative.

If no nonbasic column has $d_{ij}<0$, then $A^{\mathsf T}q\ge0$: the basic columns give the coordinates of $e_i$, and every nonbasic column has nonnegative $i$th transformed entry. Also $b^{\mathsf T}q=e_i^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}b=x_{B_i}<0$. By [F3], $q$ is a Farkas infeasibility certificate; any feasible $x\ge0$ would give $b^{\mathsf T}q=x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}q\ge0$, a contradiction.

If the basis is primal feasible, its basic vector $x$ and dual-feasible $y$ satisfy $c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y$, because $c_B^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}b=y^{\mathsf T}b$. For every feasible $z$, $A^{\mathsf T}y\le c$ and $z\ge0$ imply $c^{\mathsf T}z\ge b^{\mathsf T}y=c^{\mathsf T}x$, so $x$ is optimal. The algorithm's budget-exhausted branch asserts no further mathematical conclusion.

derivations.claim: Let $D_{ii}=-1$ when $b_i<0$ and $D_{ii}=1$ otherwise. Since $D$ is invertible and $D^{-1}=D$, $Ax=b$ is equivalent to $DAx=Db$, and $Db\ge0$. The augmented matrix $[DA\ I]$ has full row rank because it contains the identity columns; $x=0,u=Db$ is feasible for the Phase I problem and has objective $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Db\ge0$.

By [F2] the Phase I primal algorithm terminates at an optimum or an unbounded ray. Its objective is $\sum_i u_i\ge0$ at every feasible point, so a negative-cost ray is impossible; it terminates at a minimum with nonnegative reduced costs.

Suppose the minimum $w^*>0$. Any feasible original $x$ would give a Phase I feasible point $(x,u=0)$ of objective zero, contradicting minimality. Let $y$ be the terminal basis multiplier for the Phase I objective $(0,\mathbf1)$. Nonnegative reduced costs on the original columns, using [F3], give $(DA)^{\mathsf T}y\le0$, and the basic-vector identity gives $(Db)^{\mathsf T}y=w^*>0$.

Set $q=-D^{\mathsf T}y$. Then $A^{\mathsf T}q=-(DA)^{\mathsf T}y\ge0$ and $b^{\mathsf T}q=-(Db)^{\mathsf T}y<0$, so [F4] identifies it as a Farkas certificate. For any $x\ge0$ with $Ax=b$, these inequalities would imply $b^{\mathsf T}q=x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}q\ge0$, a contradiction.

Suppose instead that $w^*=0$. Since every artificial variable is nonnegative and their sum is zero, each artificial variable has value zero, and the original coordinates satisfy $DAx=Db$. If an artificial variable is basic at tableau row $k$ and some original nonbasic column has a nonzero coefficient in row $k$ of $B^{-1}DA$, pivot that column in. The pivot is nonzero, and the entering variable and leaving artificial variable both have value zero, so the represented feasible point is unchanged and one artificial basic variable is removed.

If no original nonbasic column has a nonzero coefficient in row $k$, every original basic column has a unit column there at a different row, so the entire row $k$ of $B^{-1}DA$ is zero. Every nonbasic artificial variable is zero, every other basic artificial column has zero in row $k$, and the basic artificial value at row $k$ is zero; hence row $k$ of $B^{-1}Db$ is also zero. The transformed equation is $0=0$ and may be deleted without changing the feasible set; deleting that row and its artificial basis column leaves an invertible identity submatrix for the remaining basis.

Each pivot or row deletion removes one artificial basic variable, so after at most $m$ such operations no artificial variable remains basic. The remaining basis consists of original columns and is invertible for the retained row-reduced system; its basic vector is feasible because the represented point never changed. The retained equations are equivalent to the original system by the invertible row operations and deletion only of $0=0$ rows. This proves the zero-optimum extraction claim, including redundant-row removal.

citations.quote: Add artificial variables $u\in\mathbb R^m$ and solve the Phase I problem $\min\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}u$ subject to $\widetilde A x+u=\widetilde b$, $x,u\ge0$, starting at $x=0,u=\widetilde b$ with artificial basis $I_m$.

If the minimum is positive, its returned vector yields a Farkas infeasibility certificate, as defined in [[def-revised-simplex-standard-form-linear-program]], with $A^{\mathsf T}q\ge0$ and $b^{\mathsf T}q<0$.

derivations.claim: The third right-hand side is negative, so $D=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-1)$ gives $\widetilde A=DA=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\1&1&-1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\widetilde b=Db=(1,1,3)^{\mathsf T}$. The Phase I point $x=(1,1,0)$, $u=(0,0,1)$ satisfies $\widetilde A x+u=\widetilde b$ and has objective $1$.

The Phase I dual vector $y=(-1,-1,1)$ satisfies $\widetilde A^{\mathsf T}y=(0,0,-1)^{\mathsf T}\le0$ and $\widetilde b^{\mathsf T}y=1$. For any Phase I feasible $(x,u)$, its objective $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}u$ is at least $\widetilde b^{\mathsf T}y=1$ by multiplying the constraints by $y$ and using $\widetilde A^{\mathsf T}y\le0$, $u\ge0$, and $y\le\mathbf1$. Thus the displayed feasible point attains the Phase I optimum $1>0$.

The original Farkas vector is $q=-D^{\mathsf T}y=(1,1,1)$. Direct calculation gives $A^{\mathsf T}q=(0,0,1)^{\mathsf T}\ge0$ and $b^{\mathsf T}q=1+1-3=-1<0$. Hence no $x\ge0$ can satisfy $Ax=b$, as also follows from [F2].
